target: AG1’s claim that alternative energies can effectively replace fossil fuels because several countries already have very high renewable penetration and we already have the needed knowledge and tools.
objection: High renewable shares in a few countries do not prove that alternatives can replace fossil fuels at the scale and reliability needed for large, fossil-dependent countries; U.S. alternative energy use has never exceeded about 20%, which undercuts the claim of broadly proven feasibility.

target: AG1’s use of Iceland, Paraguay, Costa Rica, and Norway as evidence that renewable transitions are generally achievable.
objection: Those countries are not a general demonstration that large, complex economies can be fully run on renewables, because their results depend on special geography, existing hydro resources, or small-system characteristics that do not straightforwardly scale to bigger countries.

target: AG1’s suggestion that nuclear energy can quickly and safely help replace fossil fuels as a low-carbon alternative.
objection: Nuclear energy is too dangerous and ineffective to be a serious global-warming solution, because accidents such as Fukushima can eliminate the carbon-free electricity gains and create major downstream harms.

target: AG2’s claim that alternative energies have not shown they can effectively replace fossil fuels at the needed scale and reliability.
objection: That claim is false because several countries already operate at very high renewable penetration—such as Iceland, Paraguay, Costa Rica, and Norway—showing that reliable large-scale renewable electricity systems are already functioning in practice.

target: AG2’s assumption that the high-renewable countries do not count as relevant evidence because they are too unusual or not representative.
objection: The examples are not all the same kind of special case: some are geothermal-heavy, some hydro-heavy, and they show different renewable mixes can support very high grid penetration. So the argument that they are just non-generalizable outliers is overstated.

target: AG2’s claim that wind and solar must be inherently unreliable and therefore cannot replace fossil fuels without ongoing fossil backup.
objection: Replacement does not depend on wind and solar alone; real power systems use diversified renewable portfolios, transmission, storage, demand response, and firm low-carbon sources like hydro, geothermal, and nuclear to maintain reliability, so fossil fuels are not inherently necessary as the only gap-filler.

target: AG2’s view that nuclear cannot serve as a firm low-carbon option for rapid fossil replacement because it is too dangerous.
objection: Nuclear is a low-carbon source of steady firm electricity that can help replace fossil fuels quickly while using far less land than widespread renewables, so dismissing it removes an important reliability tool from the transition.

target: AG1’s reliance on nuclear as a steady firm low-carbon complement that can enable rapid fossil replacement.
objection: That reliance assumes nuclear is sufficiently safe and dependable, but Fukushima shows that catastrophic accidents can wipe out the expected carbon-free benefit and impose large harms, so nuclear cannot be treated as a robust scalability solution in the timeframe discussed.

target: AG1’s portfolio argument that diversified renewables plus storage, transmission, and firm low-carbon sources can replace fossil fuels without needing natural gas.
objection: The portfolio claim assumes, without proof, that these mechanisms can be scaled to eliminate fossil-fuel generation in large countries; the examples cited do not generalize well to big incumbent grids, so the argument overstates how far such portfolios have actually displaced fossil backup requirements.

target: AG1’s use of Iceland, Paraguay, Costa Rica, and Norway as evidence that the portfolio approach can work broadly.
objection: Those examples benefit from special conditions—especially strong hydro advantages or favorable geography—and often involve smaller, more controllable grids than large fossil-dependent economies, so they do not establish that the same approach will work at scale elsewhere.
